[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#executive-summary]

## Executive Summary

This guide translates the governance framework established in the parent white paper into concrete, hands-on implementation guidance. Its goal is simple: give repository administrators, EA practice leads, and team members a clear, tiered picture of what to do — organized by how critical each item is, not by how comprehensive the list is.

**Three Tiers, One Direction:**

| Tier | Label | When | Who | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tier 1** | Critical — Do These First | Before expanding access | Repo admin + EA lead | **~2–4 hours** — mostly UI settings, no new tooling |
| **Tier 2** | Important — Do These Soon | Within the first 90 days | Repo admin + IT/Security | **~1–3 weeks elapsed** (4–8 hrs work, but IT coordination required) |
| **Tier 3** | Good to Have — Grow Into These | As the practice matures | EA + Security teams | **High** — requires tooling, budget, dedicated implementation |

**What This Document Does Not Do:**

This is not a compliance checklist that must be 100% complete before any work happens. It is practical guidance. If you are an afternoon away from finishing Tier 1, that is a good afternoon's work. If Tier 3 items are aspirational for now, that is fine — they will be here when the team is ready.

### What This Document Covers

This implementation guide provides practical, step-by-step guidance for securing the `mygainwell/eap-ref-architecture` GitHub repository and the broader `mygainwell` GitHub organization. It covers:

- Repository and organization configuration settings
- Access management practices for employees, new hires, contractors, and external partners
- Lightweight operational procedures that do not require a dedicated security team to execute
- A tiered priority model that separates must-do from nice-to-have

### Relationship to the Parent Governance Document

This guide is the operational companion to the [GitHub Repository Security Governance](github-repository-security-governance.md) white paper. The governance document establishes the _why_ and the _what_ — the to-be state, the principles, the role definitions, and the MVP framework. This document provides the _how_ — specific settings, step-by-step procedures, and practical templates.

When the two documents differ in detail, the governance document takes precedence for strategic decisions. This guide takes precedence for day-to-day implementation.

[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#tier-1-critical-controls--do-these-first]

## Tier 1: Critical Controls — Do These First

> These controls should be in place **before** access is expanded to new hires or external contributors. They are largely native GitHub capabilities — no additional tooling required. A repository admin with org admin access can implement most of these in a single working session.
>
> **Estimated effort: 2–4 hours total.** Most tasks are point-and-click in GitHub settings. The two items that require the most thought are the CODEOWNERS file (who owns which content areas?) and the GitHub Teams structure (which teams to create and who goes in each one). Everything else is configuration.
>
> **The minimum floor — what suffices right now:** If the team needs a baseline security posture today and can only do five things, do these:
>
> 1. Set repository visibility to **internal**
> 2. Enable **branch protection on `main`** with at least 1 required PR review
> 3. Enable **secret scanning and push protection** (two toggles)
> 4. Create a **CODEOWNERS file** with current content owners
> 5. Confirm **SAML SSO is enforced** at the org level (one conversation with IT)
>
> That is a defensible, auditable baseline. Everything else in this tier strengthens it further.
page_texts.9:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#21-organization-level-foundations]

### 2.1 Organization-Level Foundations

These settings live at the `mygainwell` organization level. Coordinate with your GitHub organization administrator to confirm or configure each one.
page_texts.10:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#saml-sso--enforce-do-not-just-enable]

#### SAML SSO — Enforce, Do Not Just Enable

**Why this matters:** "Enabled" SSO means users _can_ authenticate via Gainwell's identity provider. "Enforced" SSO means they _must_. Without enforcement, a personal GitHub account can still be added to the org, which bypasses all identity controls.

**What to do:**

1. Navigate to `mygainwell` → Settings → Authentication security
2. Confirm SAML SSO is configured with Gainwell's identity provider (Azure AD or Okta)
3. If SAML is enabled but not enforced, plan a short communication to current org members (they will need to re-authenticate via SSO), then enable enforcement
4. Confirm that access for users who have not SSO-authenticated is automatically revoked after enforcement

**Expected disruption:** Minimal. Any existing member who has already linked their Gainwell identity will not notice a change. Only personal-account access that was previously permitted will be blocked.

---
page_texts.11:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#mfa--required-for-all-members-and-outside-collaborators]

#### MFA — Required for All Members and Outside Collaborators

**Why this matters:** MFA is the single most effective control against credential-based account takeover. Without it, a stolen or guessed password is sufficient to access the repository.

**What to do:**

1. Navigate to `mygainwell` → Settings → Authentication security
2. Enable "Require two-factor authentication for everyone in your organization"
3. Allow 24-48 hours for existing members to comply before enforcement removes non-compliant accounts
4. Communicate the requirement and deadline clearly — provide a brief setup guide if not everyone is familiar with GitHub 2FA options

**Note:** If your organization already enforces MFA through Azure AD Conditional Access and SSO is enforced, GitHub's per-user MFA may be satisfied automatically. Verify with your identity team before sending duplicate communications.

---
page_texts.12:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#repository-default-visibility-private-or-internal]

#### Repository Default Visibility: Private or Internal

**Why this matters:** New repositories created by org members inherit the organization's default visibility. If the default is Public, content can be accidentally exposed before any review occurs.

**What to do:**

1. Navigate to `mygainwell` → Settings → Member privileges
2. Set "Default repository permission" to **None** or **Read** (not Write)
3. Set "Repository creation" to admin-only or limit to internal/private only
4. Confirm `eap-ref-architecture` is set to **Private** (preferred) or **Internal**

**Private vs. Internal:** Private limits access to explicitly added teams and users. Internal makes the repo visible to all org members (authenticated to the org). For `eap-ref-architecture`, Private is recommended — visibility should be opt-in, not opt-out.

---
page_texts.13:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#outside-collaborator-restriction]

#### Outside Collaborator Restriction

**Why this matters:** Without this restriction, any org member can invite an outside collaborator to any repository they have admin access to. This creates an uncontrolled path for external access.

**What to do:**

1. Navigate to `mygainwell` → Settings → Member privileges
2. Set "Allow outside collaborators to be invited" to **org admins only**
3. This ensures all external access is explicitly reviewed before it is granted

---
page_texts.14:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#22-repository-configuration-baseline]

### 2.2 Repository Configuration Baseline

The following settings apply directly to the `eap-ref-architecture` repository. These are configurable by a repository admin without org admin access.
page_texts.15:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#branch-protection-on-main]

#### Branch Protection on `main`

**Why this matters:** Without branch protection, any team member with Write access can push directly to `main`, bypassing peer review and creating an unauditable change history.

**Recommended configuration:**

Navigate to `eap-ref-architecture` → Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule:

| Setting | Recommended Value |
|---|---|
| Branch name pattern | `main` |
| Require a pull request before merging | Enabled |
| Required approvals | 1 (minimum); 2 for significant content changes |
| Dismiss stale PR approvals when new commits are pushed | Enabled |
| Require review from Code Owners | Enabled (once CODEOWNERS file is in place) |
| Allow force pushes | Disabled |
| Allow deletions | Disabled |

**One reviewer is usually enough.** The goal is a second set of eyes, not a committee. If your team is small, requiring 2 approvals on every PR will slow things down without meaningfully improving quality.

---
page_texts.16:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#secret-scanning-and-push-protection]

#### Secret Scanning and Push Protection

**Why this matters:** Developers occasionally commit credentials, API keys, or tokens accidentally. Secret scanning detects these after the fact; push protection blocks them before they land. Both should be enabled.

**What to do:**

1. Navigate to `eap-ref-architecture` → Settings → Code security and analysis
2. Enable **Secret scanning**
3. Enable **Push protection**
4. Review the list of supported secret types — GitHub covers the most common credential formats out of the box

**Push protection behavior:** When a contributor pushes a commit containing a detected secret, the push is blocked and they receive guidance on how to remove the secret and proceed. This is designed to be a helpful guardrail, not an obstacle. Contributors can bypass it with a justification for legitimate edge cases (e.g., example or test data that merely resembles a credential).

---
page_texts.17:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#codeowners-file]

#### CODEOWNERS File

**Why this matters:** A `CODEOWNERS` file associates specific repository paths with designated reviewers. When a PR changes files in a CODEOWNERS-defined path, the relevant owner is automatically requested as a reviewer — removing the need to remember who owns what.

**Recommended approach for `eap-ref-architecture`:**

Create a `CODEOWNERS` file in the repository root (or `.github/CODEOWNERS`). Map content areas to GitHub teams or named individuals:

```
# eap-ref-architecture CODEOWNERS
# Adjust to reflect your actual team structure

# Default owner for anything not explicitly listed below
*                               @mygainwell/ea-maintainers

# Foundation and governance materials
/foundation/                    @mygainwell/ea-maintainers
/governance/                    @mygainwell/ea-maintainers
/guiding-principles/            @mygainwell/ea-maintainers

# Business domain content
/business-portfolio/            @mygainwell/ea-contributors

# Decisions, patterns, standards
/decisions/                     @mygainwell/ea-contributors
/patterns/                      @mygainwell/ea-contributors
/standards/                     @mygainwell/ea-contributors

# Strategy and white papers — extra care here
/strategy/                      @mygainwell/ea-maintainers

# Security content — notify security team
/strategy/white-papers/security/  @mygainwell/ea-maintainers
```

Keep CODEOWNERS updated as the team evolves. An outdated CODEOWNERS file assigns reviews to the wrong people, which is counterproductive.

---
page_texts.18:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#dependency-graph-and-dependabot-alerts]

#### Dependency Graph and Dependabot Alerts

**Why this matters:** Architecture documentation often references tooling, SDKs, and platforms. If those dependencies have known vulnerabilities, the team should know about it.

**What to do:**

1. Navigate to `eap-ref-architecture` → Settings → Code security and analysis
2. Enable **Dependency graph**
3. Enable **Dependabot alerts**

For a primarily documentation repository, these are low-overhead and provide a useful signal without requiring significant automation.

---
page_texts.19:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#23-access-structure-github-teams]

### 2.3 Access Structure: GitHub Teams

**Why this matters:** Individual user access grants are harder to manage, harder to review, and harder to remove consistently than team-based grants. As team membership changes, permissions update automatically — no per-user administration required.

**Recommended team structure for `eap-ref-architecture`:**

| Team Name | Permission Level | Who Belongs |
|---|---|---|
| `ea-readers` | Read | New hires (ramp-up period), business stakeholders, executives, view-only partners |
| `ea-contributors` | Write | Active EA practice members contributing and reviewing content |
| `ea-maintainers` | Maintain | Senior architects, team leads, content area owners |
| `ea-admins` | Admin | Repository owners only — target 2-3 individuals maximum |

**Implementation steps:**

1. Navigate to `mygainwell` → Teams
2. Create each team with a clear name and description
3. Add appropriate members to each team
4. Navigate to `eap-ref-architecture` → Settings → Collaborators and teams
5. Add each team with the appropriate permission level
6. Remove any existing individual user grants now covered by team membership

**Keep `ea-admins` small.** Admin access allows changing branch protection rules, managing webhooks, and modifying security settings. The goal is 2-3 people — enough redundancy to avoid a single point of failure, not so many that admin access becomes a meaningless distinction.

---
page_texts.20:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#24-quarterly-access-review-cadence]

### 2.4 Quarterly Access Review Cadence

**Why this matters:** Access that is not reviewed accumulates. People change roles, contractors finish engagements, team structure shifts — but repository permissions often do not. A regular review catches this drift before it becomes a problem or an audit finding.

**What "quarterly" means in practice:**

A quarterly access review does not require a formal meeting or elaborate process. It is a GitHub audit, done every 3 months, answering four questions:

1. Who currently has access (at what level)?
2. Is everyone still in the right role or team?
3. Are there any outside collaborators whose engagements have ended?
4. Are there any accounts that have not been active in 60+ days?

**Recommended minimal process:**

1. Export the current collaborator and team member list from `eap-ref-architecture` → Settings → Collaborators and teams (or use the GitHub org audit log)
2. Walk the list against the current team roster — flag any mismatches
3. For outside collaborators, confirm with their access sponsor that the engagement is still active
4. Remove or downgrade access that is no longer needed
5. Record the review date and findings (even a simple GitHub issue comment is sufficient for audit purposes)

Set a recurring calendar reminder. The review itself should take 30-60 minutes for a repository of this size when team changes are modest.

---
page_texts.21:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#tier-2-important-controls--do-these-soon]

## Tier 2: Important Controls — Do These Soon

> Tier 2 controls add meaningful value and should be implemented within the first 90 days. Most require some coordination with IT or the Security team, but none require significant budget or new tooling.
>
> **Estimated effort: 4–8 hours of actual work, spread across 1–3 weeks elapsed time.** The delay is not complexity — it is coordination. SCIM integration and audit log streaming require IT and Security team involvement. If Gainwell already has SCIM configured for other enterprise applications, the GitHub-side configuration is straightforward. If not, plan for an IT work item and a lead time of 1–2 weeks. CONTRIBUTING.md and the access review record can be done independently in a few hours.
page_texts.22:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#31-identity-lifecycle-integration]

### 3.1 Identity Lifecycle Integration

**What it is:** Connecting GitHub org membership to your identity provider (Azure AD or Okta) via SCIM, so that when someone is onboarded or offboarded in the IdP, their GitHub access is automatically provisioned or removed.

**Why it matters:** Manual offboarding is the most common access hygiene failure. When someone leaves or changes roles, GitHub access gets overlooked. SCIM integration makes this automatic.

**How to approach it:**

SCIM provisioning for GitHub Enterprise is supported natively via Azure AD and Okta. The configuration requires:

- A GitHub Enterprise license (which provides SCIM endpoint support)
- A provisioned SCIM application in your IdP configured to match your GitHub org
- A mapping from IdP groups to GitHub teams

Work with your IT identity team to set this up. It is a one-time configuration that pays dividends indefinitely — every new hire and every departure is handled automatically without a manual GitHub step.

**If SCIM is not available yet:** Document a manual offboarding procedure and ensure HR or IT Operations notifies the GitHub org admin on the same day any departures occur. The notification is a process control, not a technical one, but it is meaningfully better than nothing while SCIM is being configured.

---
page_texts.23:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#32-audit-log-visibility]

### 3.2 Audit Log Visibility

**What it is:** Streaming the `mygainwell` GitHub organization's audit log to Gainwell's centralized SIEM or logging platform, so that access and activity events are visible to the security operations team without requiring them to log into GitHub directly.

**Why it matters:** GitHub's native audit log is comprehensive but it is only retained for 90-180 days (depending on Enterprise tier). For healthcare regulatory purposes, longer retention is expected. SIEM streaming also enables alerting and correlation with other security signals.

**How to approach it:**

1. Navigate to `mygainwell` → Settings → Audit log → Log streaming
2. Configure a streaming destination (GitHub supports Azure Event Hubs, Splunk, Datadog, S3, and others)
3. Coordinate with Gainwell's Security Operations team to confirm the destination and any ingestion pipeline setup required
4. Confirm that log retention in the SIEM meets the regulatory minimum (7 years for healthcare data governance audit trails is a common benchmark)

**What to monitor for, at minimum:** Admin permission changes, outside collaborator additions and removals, branch protection setting changes, secret scanning alerts, and bulk content downloads.

---
page_texts.24:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#33-onboarding-process-documentation]

### 3.3 Onboarding Process Documentation

**What it is:** A simple, maintained guide — ideally a `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `SECURITY.md` in the repository itself — that tells new contributors what to expect, what the rules of the road are, and how to get help.

**Why it matters:** Without clear documentation, new team members make avoidable mistakes: committing secrets, requesting the wrong access level, bypassing the PR process, or not knowing how to report a concern. Written guidance prevents these issues and scales to every new contributor without requiring a dedicated person to explain things.

**Recommended content for CONTRIBUTING.md:**

```markdown
# Contributing to eap-ref-architecture

## Getting Access

Access is managed through GitHub Teams. Contact your team lead or the EA practice
administrator to be added to the appropriate team. If you are a contractor or
external partner, your Gainwell sponsor will coordinate access.

## What to Commit — And What Not To

This repository contains internal Gainwell architecture content.
Please do not commit:
- Credentials, API keys, tokens, or passwords of any kind
- Customer PHI or PII
- Content marked "Do Not Distribute" or "Confidential — Not for External Use"
- Personally identifiable employee information

Secret scanning and push protection are active — accidental credential commits
will be caught before they land, but please do not rely on automation to catch
things that human judgment should prevent.

## Pull Request Process

All changes to `main` go through a pull request. At least one reviewer is required.
The CODEOWNERS file assigns reviewers automatically based on the content area you are
modifying. Do not merge your own PRs unless you are performing an administrative action
with explicit approval.

## Security Concerns

If you discover something that looks like a security issue — an accidentally committed
credential, content visible to people who should not see it, or anything else that
concerns you — contact [security contact or Slack channel] immediately.
Do not wait; do not try to fix it quietly on your own.
```

**Recommended content for SECURITY.md:**

A brief file pointing to the security reporting contact and reinforcing that credential exposure should be reported immediately. GitHub surfaces this file prominently when users navigate to the repository's Security tab.

---
page_texts.25:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#34-structured-access-review-process]

### 3.4 Structured Access Review Process

**What it is:** A slightly more formalized version of the quarterly access review described in Tier 1, with a documented record and a defined owner.

**Why it matters:** The Tier 1 quarterly cadence is the habit; the Tier 2 structured process is the documentation. For HIPAA and SOC 2 purposes, you will want evidence that access reviews actually occurred and what was done as a result. A lightweight record is sufficient.

**Recommended lightweight process:**

Maintain a GitHub issue in a governance or operations repository (or in `eap-ref-architecture` under a dedicated label) with the following structure for each quarterly review:

```
Access Review — Q[X] [Year]
Date: [Date]
Reviewer: [Name]

Teams reviewed:
- ea-readers: [X] members — [any changes made]
- ea-contributors: [X] members — [any changes made]
- ea-maintainers: [X] members — [any changes made]
- ea-admins: [X] members — [any changes made]

Outside collaborators reviewed: [X] — [any removed]
Dormant accounts (60+ days inactive): [X] — [action taken]

Next review due: [Date]
Notes: [anything notable]
```

This creates a dated, auditable record without requiring a formal report or dedicated tooling.

---
page_texts.26:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#tier-3-good-to-have--grow-into-these]

## Tier 3: Good to Have — Grow Into These

> These are capabilities worth aspiring to as the practice matures. The team can operate securely and responsibly with only Tiers 1 and 2 in place. These become relevant when the team is larger, the content is more sensitive, or compliance requirements escalate.
>
> **Estimated effort: High — do not start these until Tiers 1 and 2 are stable.** Config-as-code (Terraform), DLP integration, behavioral analytics, and just-in-time access all require dedicated tooling, platform dependencies, and in most cases budget approval and a proper implementation project. None of these are a half-day task. They are included here so the team knows where to grow — not as immediate obligations.
page_texts.27:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#41-configuration-as-code]

### 4.1 Configuration as Code

Define repository security configuration (branch protection, team membership, security settings) as infrastructure code managed through a reviewed workflow:

- **GitHub Terraform Provider:** Automate repository creation, team management, and branch protection settings at scale
- **GitHub Actions Workflows:** Automated compliance checks that validate security configuration on a schedule and alert on configuration drift
- **Repository Templates:** Pre-configured templates that apply the Tier 1 security baseline automatically when new repositories are created

**When this makes sense:** When you manage 5+ repositories, when multiple administrators apply changes independently, or when configuration drift has caused issues. For a single repository with 2-3 admins, manual configuration governance is sufficient.

---
page_texts.28:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#42-data-loss-prevention-integration]

### 4.2 Data Loss Prevention Integration

Connect GitHub to Gainwell's enterprise DLP platform to inspect repository content for sensitive data patterns (PHI, PII, proprietary identifiers) and either alert or block commits containing them.

**When this makes sense:** When the repository begins containing content that intersects with customer data, regulated information, or material with specific contractual restrictions on storage location. Pure architecture documentation (standards, patterns, guidance) is lower priority for DLP than repositories containing operational or customer data.

**Practical note:** GitHub's native secret scanning and push protection cover the highest-risk category (credentials) already. DLP adds coverage for content-level sensitive data patterns, which requires more configuration and tuning to avoid excessive false positives.

---
page_texts.29:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#43-behavioral-analytics-and-ueba]

### 4.3 Behavioral Analytics and UEBA

Deploy User and Entity Behavior Analytics that baseline normal GitHub access patterns and alert on anomalies:

- Bulk repository clones or downloads above baseline
- Access from unusual geographic locations or at unusual hours
- Rapid permission escalation activity
- Unusual commit patterns from accounts that typically only read

**When this makes sense:** When the repository contains genuinely sensitive strategic content, when contractor volume is high enough that manual monitoring is impractical, or when the organization has experienced a security incident and wants enhanced detection capability.

**Practical note:** Most SIEM platforms can provide basic anomaly detection using GitHub audit log streaming (Tier 2). Dedicated UEBA adds ML-based baselining but also adds cost and operational overhead. Start with rule-based alerting from the audit log and move to UEBA when you find that rules are missing events you care about.

---
page_texts.30:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#44-just-in-time-privileged-access]

### 4.4 Just-in-Time Privileged Access

Replace standing admin access with time-limited, approval-based privilege elevation:

- Admin-level access is not permanently held by anyone
- When administrative tasks are needed, a privileged access request is submitted and approved
- Access is granted for a defined window (e.g., 2 hours) and automatically expires

**When this makes sense:** When `ea-admins` membership exceeds 3-4 people, when admin actions are infrequent enough that standing access is wasteful, or when a compliance framework specifically requires no standing privileged access.

**Practical note:** For most EA repository contexts, keeping admin access to 2-3 named, trusted individuals is sufficient. JIT access adds process overhead that may not be justified unless there is a specific compliance or audit driver.

---
page_texts.32:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#51-onboarding-a-new-full-time-employee]

### 5.1 Onboarding a New Full-Time Employee

**Who does this:** Team lead or EA practice administrator, in coordination with the new hire's manager.

**Step 1 — Confirm organizational identity is active**

The employee should have a `@gainwelltechnologies.com` account provisioned and SSO configured. If they can log in to other Gainwell systems using their corporate identity, GitHub SSO should work. If there is an issue, resolve identity provisioning before proceeding.

**Step 2 — Determine the right team**

| If the new hire will... | Add to team |
|---|---|
| Browse content to ramp up, no immediate contributions | `ea-readers` |
| Actively contribute architecture content | `ea-contributors` |
| Lead a content area, act as reviewer, maintain quality | `ea-maintainers` |

Err toward `ea-readers` for the first few weeks. It is straightforward to upgrade to `ea-contributors` once they are oriented.

**Step 3 — Add them to the team**

Navigate to `mygainwell` → Teams → [appropriate team] → Members → Add a member. Search by their GitHub username or email.

**Step 4 — Send a brief orientation note**

Point them to:

- The `CONTRIBUTING.md` file in the repository root
- The `README.md` for an overview of how content is organized
- Your team's preferred Slack or Teams channel for architecture collaboration

**Step 5 — Record the access grant**

Log the access in your tracking record (GitHub issue, team wiki, or spreadsheet). Include: name, team assigned, date, and who requested and approved the access.

---
page_texts.33:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#52-onboarding-a-contractor-or-external-contributor]

### 5.2 Onboarding a Contractor or External Contributor

**Who does this:** Internal access sponsor, with support from the repo admin.

**Before anything else — three questions to confirm:**

1. **Is the IP protection covered?** Does the contractor's services agreement or NDA include the intellectual property in this repository? If uncertain, coordinate with legal or procurement before proceeding.

2. **Is there a named internal sponsor?** A specific Gainwell employee should own responsibility for this person's access — requesting it, confirming it at the 90-day mark, and requesting removal when the engagement ends.

3. **What access do they actually need?** Read access is the default. Write access requires a specific deliverable that justifies it.

**Access steps:**

1. Navigate to `eap-ref-architecture` → Settings → Collaborators and teams → Add outside collaborator
2. Enter their GitHub username (they must have an existing GitHub account)
3. Select the appropriate permission level:

| Permission | Default? | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| Read | Yes — default | Most reviewing or reference work |
| Write | No — requires justification | Specific contribution deliverable |
| Maintain | Never | Not for outside collaborators |
| Admin | Never | Not for outside collaborators |

1. Set a calendar reminder for a 90-day access check-in

**During the engagement:**

At 90 days, the sponsor confirms access is still needed or requests removal. Maximum duration without a sponsor-confirmed renewal is 180 days.

**At the end of the engagement:**

The sponsor notifies the repo admin, who removes the outside collaborator via Settings → Collaborators and teams → [collaborator name] → Remove. Target same-day removal.

---
page_texts.34:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#53-conducting-an-access-review]

### 5.3 Conducting an Access Review

**When:** Quarterly — set a recurring calendar reminder at a consistent cadence (e.g., first week of each quarter).

**Who:** Repository admin, confirmed by the EA practice lead.

**Step 1 — Export the current access state**

Navigate to `eap-ref-architecture` → Settings → Collaborators and teams. Review:

- All teams and their member counts
- Any individual collaborators (should be outside collaborators only)
- Permission levels for each team

**Step 2 — Ask four questions per person**

1. Is this person still in a role that requires this level of access?
2. For contributors and maintainers: have they been active in the repository in the past 90 days?
3. For outside collaborators: is the engagement still active, per the sponsor?
4. Does their permission level match their current responsibilities?

**Step 3 — Make adjustments**

- Remove outside collaborators whose engagements have ended
- Downgrade team members whose roles have changed
- Flag dormant accounts (60+ days no activity) for confirmation before removing

**Step 4 — Record the review**

A brief GitHub issue comment is sufficient. Capture the date, who reviewed, what was found, and what changed.

---
page_texts.35:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#54-handling-a-security-concern]

### 5.4 Handling a Security Concern

**The right response to most security concerns: surface it promptly. Do not wait, and do not try to fix it silently.**
page_texts.36:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#accidentally-committed-credential]

#### Accidentally Committed Credential

1. **Rotate the credential immediately** — assume it is compromised regardless of whether anyone has accessed it
2. If push protection caught it before the push landed: the commit never entered the repository; no scrubbing required
3. If it is already in repository history: remove it from the current codebase (new commit), then scrub the history using `git filter-repo` or contact the GitHub org admin for assistance
4. Notify IT Security that remediation is in progress
5. Rotate the credential regardless of remediation status

---
page_texts.37:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#someone-has-access-they-should-not-have]

#### Someone Has Access They Should Not Have

1. Remove or downgrade the access immediately — do not wait for a review cycle
2. Pull the audit log to see what they have accessed recently
3. If the access pattern looks routine: this was an administrative oversight — document and move on
4. If the access pattern looks unusual (bulk downloads, after-hours access to sensitive paths, permission escalation): escalate to Information Security

---
page_texts.38:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#suspected-account-compromise]

#### Suspected Account Compromise

1. Suspend the user's GitHub org membership immediately (prevents access without deleting history)
2. Contact the user through an out-of-band channel (phone or alternate email) to verify their identity
3. If unauthorized access is confirmed: force a password reset and MFA re-enrollment via the identity provider
4. Pull the audit log for the period in question and document what was accessed
5. Notify Information Security — this is a formal security incident
6. Restore access after credential reset and user identity verification

---
page_texts.39:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#repository-configuration-changed-without-authorization]

#### Repository Configuration Changed Without Authorization

1. Restore the correct configuration immediately (branch protection, visibility, etc.)
2. Pull the audit log to identify who made the change and when
3. If the change was inadvertent (admin error): correct and document
4. If the change appears unauthorized: escalate to Information Security
5. Review `ea-admins` membership — is admin access still appropriately restricted?

---
page_texts.40:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#risk-and-trade-off-considerations]

## Risk and Trade-Off Considerations

Security controls involve trade-offs. This section identifies the most common ones so teams can make informed decisions.
page_texts.41:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#speed-vs-control-access-approval-friction]

### Speed vs. Control: Access Approval Friction

**The tension:** A formal multi-step approval for every access request improves accountability but slows onboarding and creates bottlenecks when approvers are unavailable.

**Suggested balance:** For standard roles (new employees joining the expected team), use a lightweight notification model — the team lead requests access, the repo admin grants it, and the record is logged. Reserve formal multi-step approval for unusual requests: elevated permissions, strategic-restricted content, or outside collaborators from organizations with no existing relationship.

---
page_texts.42:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#granularity-vs-maintainability-team-structure]

### Granularity vs. Maintainability: Team Structure

**The tension:** A highly granular team structure enables precise access control but creates maintenance overhead and potential configuration drift.

**Suggested balance:** The four-team structure (`ea-readers`, `ea-contributors`, `ea-maintainers`, `ea-admins`) is sufficient for most EA practice sizes. Add granularity only when there is a demonstrated need — for example, if a specific folder contains sensitive strategic content that warrants restriction even from general contributors. Do not preemptively create teams for problems that do not yet exist.

---
page_texts.43:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#detection-vs-productivity-secret-scanning-and-push-protection]

### Detection vs. Productivity: Secret Scanning and Push Protection

**The tension:** Push protection blocks commits with detected secrets. Occasionally it produces false positives — flagging content that looks like a credential but is not (test data, example values, documentation snippets).

**Suggested balance:** When a legitimate commit is blocked, contributors can bypass the block and provide a justification. This is intentionally possible for false positives. Disable push protection only as a last resort and only temporarily; instead, work through the GitHub settings to suppress specific false positive patterns.

---
page_texts.44:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#monitoring-vs-overhead-audit-log-review]

### Monitoring vs. Overhead: Audit Log Review

**The tension:** Thorough audit log review provides visibility into access patterns and potential issues, but it requires someone's time. Without SIEM streaming, manual log review is tedious at scale.

**Suggested balance:** Do not attempt to manually review the full audit log regularly. Configure specific alerts for the highest-risk events (admin permission changes, outside collaborator additions, branch protection changes) and focus manual review on the quarterly cadence and triggered alerts. Once SIEM streaming is configured (Tier 2), many of these become automated.

---
page_texts.45:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#appendix-a-access-request--github-issue-template]

## Appendix A: Access Request — GitHub Issue Template

For teams that want a lightweight, trackable access request process without a dedicated portal, this GitHub Issue template provides an auditable approach. Create the file at `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/access-request.yml` in the relevant governance repository.

```yaml
name: Repository Access Request
description: Request access to eap-ref-architecture or a change to existing access
title: "[ACCESS] <Name> - <Team Requested>"
labels: ["access-request"]
assignees: []

body:
  - type: markdown
    attributes:
      value: |
        Use this form to request access to the eap-ref-architecture repository or
        to request a change to existing access. The repository admin will process
        the request and close the issue when complete.

  - type: input
    id: requester-name
    attributes:
      label: Requestor Name
      placeholder: Full name
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: input
    id: requester-email
    attributes:
      label: Gainwell Email
      placeholder: name@gainwelltechnologies.com
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: input
    id: github-username
    attributes:
      label: GitHub Username
      placeholder: github_username
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: dropdown
    id: access-type
    attributes:
      label: Access Type
      options:
        - Full-time employee — new access
        - Full-time employee — access change
        - Contractor / external contributor — new access
        - Contractor / external contributor — access extension
        - Access removal
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: dropdown
    id: permission-level
    attributes:
      label: Permission Level Requested
      options:
        - Read (view only — default for new hires and most external contributors)
        - Write (active contributors — requires justification below)
        - Maintain (content area leads — requires explicit approval)
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: textarea
    id: justification
    attributes:
      label: Business Justification
      description: Why is this access needed? What work will this person be doing?
      placeholder: >
        e.g., "New EA practice member joining the infrastructure architecture team.
        Will contribute to standards documentation and pattern library."
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: input
    id: access-end-date
    attributes:
      label: Access End Date (contractors and external contributors only)
      description: >
        Leave blank for full-time employees. For contractors, specify the engagement
        end date or a 90-day review date, whichever is sooner.
      placeholder: YYYY-MM-DD

  - type: input
    id: sponsor
    attributes:
      label: Internal Access Sponsor (contractors and external contributors only)
      description: >
        Gainwell employee responsible for this person's access — including the
        90-day check-in and requesting removal when the engagement ends.
      placeholder: Sponsor name and email

  - type: checkboxes
    id: confirmation
    attributes:
      label: Confirmation
      options:
        - label: >
            For contractors — I confirm the contractor's services agreement or NDA
            covers the intellectual property contained in this repository
          required: false
        - label: >
            I confirm the access scope described above is the minimum necessary
            for the work to be performed
          required: true
```

[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#appendix-b-security-incident-quick-response-guide]

## Appendix B: Security Incident Quick-Response Guide

This is a fast-reference guide for the most common security scenarios. It is intentionally concise — the goal is to get to the right action quickly. For incidents involving confirmed unauthorized access or IP exposure, escalate to Information Security and follow Gainwell's enterprise incident response process.
page_texts.47:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#b1-accidentally-committed-credential]

### B.1 Accidentally Committed Credential

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Rotate the credential immediately** — assume it is compromised |
| 2 | If push protection caught it: push never landed — no scrubbing needed |
| 3 | If already in repo history: scrub with `git filter-repo` or engage GitHub support |
| 4 | Notify IT Security that remediation is complete |
| 5 | Add the credential type to `.gitignore` or move to a secrets manager |

> Never assume "nobody will find it" is an acceptable resolution. Commit history is visible to everyone with repo access, and automated scanners actively harvest credentials from git history.

---
page_texts.48:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#b2-unauthorized-or-unexpected-access-discovered]

### B.2 Unauthorized or Unexpected Access Discovered

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Remove or downgrade the access immediately |
| 2 | Pull the audit log: filter by user, review recent activity |
| 3 | Routine access pattern (low volume, normal hours): administrative oversight, document and close |
| 4 | Unusual access pattern (bulk downloads, sensitive paths, after-hours): notify Information Security |
| 5 | Document: when discovered, what was found, what action was taken |

---
page_texts.49:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#b3-suspected-account-compromise]

### B.3 Suspected Account Compromise

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Suspend the user's org membership immediately |
| 2 | Contact the user out of band (phone or alternate email) to verify identity |
| 3 | Confirmed unauthorized: force password reset + MFA re-enrollment via IdP |
| 4 | Pull audit log for the anomalous period; document what was accessed |
| 5 | Notify Information Security — this is a formal security incident |
| 6 | Restore access after credential reset and user verification |

---
page_texts.50:
[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#b4-repository-configuration-changed-without-authorization]

### B.4 Repository Configuration Changed Without Authorization

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Restore correct configuration immediately |
| 2 | Pull audit log: identify who changed what and when |
| 3 | Admin error: correct, document, move on |
| 4 | Unauthorized change: escalate to Information Security |
| 5 | Review `ea-admins` membership — is the list still appropriately small? |

---

[strategy/white-papers/security/github-repository-security-implementation.md#strategy-summary-tldr]

## Strategy Summary (TL;DR)

**Purpose:** This is the practical implementation companion to the GitHub Repository Security Governance white paper. It tells you what to do, in what order, and how important each item is.

**The Three Tiers:**

- **Tier 1 (Critical — do before expanding access):** Enforce SAML SSO. Require MFA. Set the repository to Private. Enable branch protection on `main` with required PR reviews. Enable secret scanning and push protection. Create and maintain a CODEOWNERS file. Manage all access through GitHub Teams. Run a quarterly access review.

- **Tier 2 (Important — do within 90 days):** Integrate GitHub with your IdP via SCIM for automated lifecycle management. Stream audit logs to Gainwell's SIEM. Create CONTRIBUTING.md and SECURITY.md. Formalize the quarterly access review with a written record.

- **Tier 3 (Good to have — grow into these):** Configuration-as-code for repository settings. DLP integration for content inspection. Behavioral analytics for anomaly detection. Just-in-time privileged access.

**For New Hires:** Confirm SSO is active → add to the appropriate GitHub Team (`ea-readers` to start) → point to CONTRIBUTING.md → log the grant.

**For Contractors and External Contributors:** Confirm IP protection is contractually covered → identify an internal sponsor → add as Outside Collaborator (Read by default; Write only if justified by a specific deliverable) → set a 90-day check-in reminder → log the grant with an expiration date → remove same-day when the engagement ends.

**The Access Review in One Paragraph:** Once a quarter, pull the collaborator and team member list. Ask four questions per person: Are they still here? Are they in the right role? Do they actually need this access level? For contractors — is the engagement still active? Remove or downgrade anything that does not hold up. Write a one-line record that you did it and when.

**Primary Audience:** EA Practice Leadership, Repository Administrators, Team Leads, New Hire Onboarding, Contractor Engagement Managers

**Parent Document:** [GitHub Repository Security Governance](github-repository-security-governance.md) — strategic context, to-be state architecture, role definitions, and the MVP controls framework.
